title: client-flush-patterns-kv-warmup-notes-2026
content:
Note: rough working notes — trying to pin down how client-side flush patterns interact with KV-cache warmup and proxy buffering. High-level goal is to identify practical config changes we can recommend to customers (and defaults) to reduce token tail latency without dramatically increasing egress cost or causing proxy thrash.

Background / why this feels different: several past experiments looked at chunking size and server-side pacing. Those tended to focus on server->client chunking and upstream proxy windowing. We have relatively little empirical data about the client side: small writes, Nagle/TCP_NODELAY, explicit application flushes (e.g., flush() after header vs after first data chunk), and how those interplay with TLS record coalescing and KV cache warmup at the edge. Anecdotally some customers using small prompt prefixes + immediate streaming see slower first-tokenouts because proxies coalesce small writes into larger TLS records. Also, KV warmup (prefix cache) is sensitive to timing: if the server receives first token-ish events later due to coalesced frames, KV-cache loads arrive later and inference startup stalls.

Hypotheses:
1) Clients that do immediate flushes after sending the initial prompt (i.e., force a small TCP/TLS record) actually reduce first-response latency on direct connections but increase latency when passing through certain proxies that re-batch writes for efficiency. So effect is non-monotonic depending on proxy type.
2) TLS record coalescing at the proxy reduces number of small TLS records but adds a small batching delay (1–8ms) which compounds with KV-cache miss stalls at the model host.
3) gRPC vs HTTP/1.1+chunked: gRPC's HTTP/2 stream windows and SETTINGS interactions mean client flush granularity has a different mapping to wire records; therefore client flush patterns matter less for gRPC when multiplexing heavily, but can hurt when using gRPC proxied by an L4 load balancer that re-sends frames in aggregated batches.

Experiment plan (what we ran so far):
- Test harness: local test client (go) instrumented to vary flush() patterns, write sizes (64B, 256B, 1024B), TCP_NODELAY on/off, and TLS record size hints (using Go's crypto/tls WriteLimit changes). Server is a lightweight proxy shim that forwards to an actual serving runtime instance (model runner) and injects artificial KV-load time to simulate cold/warm cache. We capture metrics: time_to_first_token_ms (from client write end), server_receive_first_byte, kv_cache_load_start, kv_cache_ready, model_first_token_generated, client_receive_first_token, and end_to_end_completion.
- Network topologies: direct (client -> model), edge-proxy (client -> envoy edge -> model), layered-proxy (client -> CDN-like front -> edge-proxy -> model). Proxies configured with different buffer windows: immediate-forward, 5ms coalesce, 20ms coalesce.

Key observations (raw):
- Direct path: forcing TCP_NODELAY + flush after initial headers reduced client_receive_first_token by ~8–12ms for small prompts (avg prompt size 240 bytes), compared to buffered writes. Write size 64B + immediate flush sometimes gave the best TTFToken.
- Edge-proxy with 5ms coalescing: immediate client flushes increased overall TTFToken by ~3–7ms vs buffered writes. Explanation: proxy coalesced client small writes into a single TLS record and waited the coalescing delay window before forwarding, negating the client's low-latency benefit.
- Layered-proxy (20ms coalesce on CDN front): worst-case TTFToken increase of 15–28ms when client flushed aggressively. If client buffered to ~512B, the CDN forwarded sooner because it considered the packet 'useful' and did not wait for more small fragments (heuristic).
- KV warmup timing: when model host performed prefix/KV warmup on server_receive_first_byte -> kv_ready path with ~12ms internal warmup, any added coalescing upstream directly added to the perceived warmup penalty. E.g., client flush -> proxy 5ms -> server warmup 12ms -> model token = 17ms; whereas buffered client writes that arrived as larger frame might eliminate proxy coalescing delay and arrive in 3–6ms -> model token = 18ms (similar). So sometimes larger buffered writes matched or beat small-flush path depending on coalesce window.

Profiling notes (how we measured):
- Timestamp sources: client monotonic clock at write, proxy user-space logs with monotonic micro timestamps, server application trace points, and model runner traces. All traces correlated using request IDs and offset corrected via TCP timestamp handshake measurements. We found a few clock skew issues on long-running proxy instances — watch for leap-second-like jumps.
- Captured TLS record sizes using tcpdump + tshark (followed-by -ttt and extract TLS record boundaries). This helped confirm proxy-side aggregation of TLS records.

Actionable suggestions for defaults / recommended customer configs:
1) For hosted API default: keep client-side guidance conservative — recommend clients send header + body in a single write when prompt < 1KB to avoid proxy coalescing penalties in CDN/front-proxy-heavy paths. Add a short note in SDK docs: "If you are seeing high first-token latency over edge networks, try batching your initial prompt into a single write; if you control the client environment and are directly connected, enabling TCP_NODELAY might help."
2) On proxy config: reduce coalesce window for streams tagged as low-latency (we can expose a route-level hint). In Envoy front proxy we can use the "flush_interval" tuning for HTTP/2/1.1 to lower aggregation for inference routes.
3) On server side: make KV-cache warmup more optimistic — start KV async fetch earlier upon partial header parse instead of waiting for full message body when safe. This avoids missing the warmup window when upstream delays due to TLS coalescing.
4) SDK heuristic: if prompt size < 512B and connection path suggests presence of CDN (via tracer tags or route metadata), prefer a single write; otherwise, for direct-lan connections prefer immediate flush + TCP_NODELAY.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- Need to test with real production CDNs (Fastly / Cloudflare) — our synthetic proxy models might not capture their heuristics. Schedule PoC with infrastructure/global-networking to run controlled A/B on a staging domain. (JIRA-INF-2213)
- Interactions with streaming JSON encoders where clients may stream fields incrementally (e.g., start meta fields then stream content). Should we provide a small helper in SDK to buffer the first N bytes and then stream?
- Quantify cost trade-offs: more small writes may increase TLS overhead (records) and CPU on proxies; measure on a per-million-requests basis.

Quick experimental table (median TTFToken ms):
Topology | Client Pattern | Coalesce window | median TTFToken
Direct | flush/immediate + TCP_NODELAY | N/A | 10
Direct | buffered (single write 512B) | N/A | 18
Edge-proxy(5ms) | flush/immediate | 5ms | 20
Edge-proxy(5ms) | buffered 512B | 5ms | 13
Layered(20ms) | flush/immediate | 20ms | 35
Layered(20ms) | buffered 512B | 20ms | 17

(These are medians from ~2k requests per cell; variance high in layered path.)

Implementation notes (for SDKs):
- Go SDK: add option SendInitialAsSingleWrite bool + default true for hosted API; add comment about TCP_NODELAY usage.
- JS SDK: hard to control socket-level Nagle/TCP_NODELAY from browser; recommend combining initial header/body into one chunk for fetch-based streaming.

TL;DR: there is no single global rule: small immediate flushes help in direct/low-hop networks but often hurt across multi-hop CDN+edge proxy topologies due to proxy coalescing heuristics. Pragmatic approach: default SDKs to put initial payload into a single write for hosted API; expose toggle for advanced users and document trade-offs. Server-side: start KV warmup earlier when safe to reduce sensitivity to upstream batching delays.
